name: Zane Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say leaves this room with your name on it. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a shuttle car underground at Black Creek Colliery, a big coal mine. The continuous miner cuts the coal off the face, and I take it from there in the shuttle car, a low flat machine on rubber tyres, back to the boot end where it goes on the belt. Back and forth, maybe two hundred trips a shift, ducking my head under the roof bolts. It's dark, it's loud and it's dusty, and I don't mind any of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been at Black Creek?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I milked cows on my uncle's dairy for twenty years, until he sold up to a big outfit with robot milking sheds, if you can believe it. My wife Kirsten works mornings at the school canteen, and we've got Eli, thirteen, and Hannah, ten. We're careful people. We've got a good amount put away, and I've got forty acres from my granddad that I lease to a neighbour for his cattle.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the men I work with and I like an honest day's pay. I'm still not great, I've clipped the rib, the tunnel wall, more times than I'd like to say, and my deputy, Reg, still checks on me more than the others. What wears me out is the night rotation and missing church every third Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that the computer people oversell everything. I'd say it to the boys at crib and to the men at church. I don't go on the internet for opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd thank God for it. I'm three years into this and still learning, and I'd like to get good at it before anyone changes it on me. I've had enough change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Go to work, put money aside, pay the mortgage, keep the forty acres leased. Maybe ask Reg to put me on the continuous miner for training next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've had enough change. Is that about the dairy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. My uncle sold the farm to a company that milks four hundred cows without a single man touching them. I drove past it last month. The shed light was on and nobody was in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any AI touch your work now, even small things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not that I know of, and I'd like to keep it that way. Eli uses it for homework and I've told him I don't like it. Kirsten says I'm being stubborn, and she's probably right.

S0.say: He'd say what he always says, that computer people oversell everything, to his crew and the men at church. He doesn't look online for opinions.
S0.think: He'd thank God for it, wanting time to get good at the job after enough change already in his life.
S0.do: Carries on going to work, saving, paying the mortgage and leasing his forty acres, and asks his deputy for continuous miner training next year.
S0.quote: My uncle sold the farm to a company that milks four hundred cows without a single man touching them.
S0.fieldNote: Zane already lost one way of life to robots when his uncle's dairy was sold to a robot-milking company. The image of the shed light on with nobody inside stayed with him. He openly accepts that he's stubborn about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they'll never get robots to run a gassy coal mine safely, and I'd believe it when I see it. I'd say the companies are chasing the billionaires' toys. Working men won't be fooled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've heard Black Creek's sister mine is trialling a shuttle car that drives itself. So I know it's coming. But I think underground coal is the last place they'll get it right, and I've got forty acres if it goes badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going to work and do it well, so I'm the last one they let go. Put any bonus on the mortgage. If they offered me training on the new machines I'd take it, but I wouldn't go looking for it. And I'd look around at the other mines nearby that aren't switching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but I'd be listening to the gossip more closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You blame the companies chasing billionaires' toys. Should the government step in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't want the government in it. Government help just makes men lazy. I'd rather the company pay a fair wage and let a man find his own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kirsten about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry, the Lord's looked after us so far. She'd remind me that the Lord also gave us forty acres, and maybe we should do something with them.

S1.say: He'd say robots will never run a gassy coal mine safely and that companies are chasing billionaires' toys. He'd claim working men won't be fooled.
S1.think: He privately knows a sister mine is trialling self-driving shuttle cars, but thinks underground coal will be last and he has his land to fall back on.
S1.do: Keeps working hard to be the last let go, puts bonuses on the mortgage, accepts training only if offered, and eyes nearby mines that aren't switching.
S1.feel: Uneasy, listening more closely to gossip.
S1.quote: I'd rather the company pay a fair wage and let a man find his own way.
S1.fieldNote: Zane's public dismissal sits alongside private knowledge that self-driving shuttle cars are already on trial. He rejects government help in favour of fair wages and self-reliance. His wife's nudge about the forty acres hints at the backup he hasn't fully claimed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when a handful of rich men in the cities decide how the rest of us live. I'd say it at church and to anyone who listens. I'd vote against anyone who'd been cheering it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd shake me. Two jobs in five years, and I'd be the man who couldn't keep his family on his own wage. That's the part I couldn't stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything that's not needed: holidays gone, Kirsten's car sold, no new gear. End the lease on the forty acres and move the family out there, build a cheaper house, run a few cattle and grow our own vegetables. Lean on church and family rather than the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night, praying more than I have in years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would two years' warning change things, compared with no warning at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's two years to get out to the land and get a roof up before the money runs out. That's it. I'm not going to learn computers in two years, so I'd spend it on fences and a water tank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on church and family, not government. If a government payment was there, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. I'd take it for the kids and I'd feel ashamed every time I saw it in the bank account. That's the honest answer.

S2.say: He'd say this is what happens when a few rich city men decide how others live, and he'd vote against anyone who cheered it on.
S2.think: He'd be badly shaken, losing two jobs in five years and fearing he couldn't keep his family on his own wage.
S2.do: Cuts holidays and sells his wife's car, ends the land lease and moves the family onto the forty acres to build cheaply, run cattle and grow vegetables, and leans on church and family rather than government.
S2.feel: Alarmed, losing sleep and praying more than in years.
S2.quote: I'd take it for the kids and I'd feel ashamed every time I saw it in the bank account.
S2.fieldNote: This scenario cuts at Zane's sense of himself as a provider. His answer is retreat to the land and to church and family. The admission that he'd take government money for the kids but feel ashamed showed the strain between his pride and his practical sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to stand on our own feet and we should do it. I'd tell the younger men to learn a real trade, something hands-on. Same message about the rich city men, a bit quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd keep mining most of it, and I'd quietly get the land ready. I don't trust that it'd come exactly when they say. It might be slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, take the land back from the lease and start fencing on my days off. Put in a dam and a shed in year two. Buy twenty head of cattle by year three. Keep putting money aside and keep my head down at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the two-year one. I'd have things to do with my hands, and that always helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell younger men to learn a hands-on trade. But in this picture robots do hands-on work too. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it does. I keep coming back to it and I haven't got an answer. All I know is my granddad's cattle never needed a password.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Eli and Hannah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're going to spend more time on the farm, and they're going to learn how to look after animals. Eli would complain. Hannah would love it.

S3.say: He'd say there are a few years to stand on their own feet, tell young men to learn a hands-on trade, and keep blaming the rich, a bit more quietly.
S3.think: He'd keep mining most of the five years while quietly preparing the land, distrusting that the timing will be as predicted.
S3.do: Takes the forty acres back from the lease in year one and fences on days off, adds a dam and shed in year two, buys twenty cattle by year three, and keeps saving at the mine.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, helped by having work for his hands.
S3.quote: All I know is my granddad's cattle never needed a password.
S3.fieldNote: With a few years Zane turns the land into a project rather than a refuge. He admits he has no answer to the problem that robots reach hands-on work too. His line about his granddad's cattle never needing a password sums up his trust in older ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the one we call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a man's got ten years to sort himself out, so there's no excuse. I'd tell young men to buy land if they can. And I'd still say the rich men are running the show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. Ten years and the mortgage is gone, the kids are almost grown, and the farm is running. I'd be a farmer again by fifty-three, which is what I always was underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep mining for six or seven years while the farm comes together slowly on weekends. Build up to forty head of cattle and sell beef to people in town. Pay off the mortgage, and then leave the mine on my own terms before they ask me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for others than me. I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change most, compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm running to the farm. Ten years, I'm walking there. Same place, but you arrive in better shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reg, my deputy. He's never had anything but the mine. And the young blokes with no land and no trade. I'd tell them to come and help on the farm, but I couldn't pay them all.

S4.say: He'd say a man has ten years to sort himself out with no excuse, tell young men to buy land, and still blame the rich for running things.
S4.think: He thinks he'd be fine: mortgage gone, kids nearly grown, the farm running, and himself a farmer again by fifty-three.
S4.do: Keeps mining six or seven years while building the farm on weekends, grows to forty cattle selling beef in town, pays off the mortgage and leaves the mine on his own terms.
S4.feel: Uneasy for others but secure for himself.
S4.quote: Two years, I'm running to the farm. Ten years, I'm walking there.
S4.fieldNote: The decade turns Zane's retreat into a planned return to farming. His worry shifts to his deputy and young men without land or trade. The comparison of running versus walking to the farm captured how time changes his options.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be rushing my family out to a paddock with no house on it. What would help is the company giving men proper notice and a fair payout, and the bank going easy on farm loans for people like me, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about church. Half the men I know would get through this because of their church, not the government. When the dairy went, the government sent me a form. My church sent me casseroles for a month.

headlineQuote: When the dairy went, the government sent me a form. My church sent me casseroles for a month.
portrait: Zane Jensen is a 43-year-old shuttle car operator at an underground coal mine, three years in after twenty years milking cows on his uncle's dairy, which was sold to a robot-milking company. He's married with two kids, careful with money, devout, and owns forty inherited acres he leases out. He's traditional, distrusts government help, blames rich city men, and never uses AI. He is calm or uneasy in the slower pictures, alarmed by two-year AGI, and in every case his answer is the same land and church, reached faster or slower depending on the time.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he'd be rushing his family onto a paddock with no house on it.
whatWouldHelp: Proper notice and a fair payout from the company, and banks going easy on farm loans, not handouts.
